case_info.scenario: A 14-year old girl presented with sudden painless vision decline in the left eye for 5 days, without vision decline in the right eye. Her visual acuity was 20/20 OU 6 months earlier. She reported constant fatigue, occasional dizziness and headache, mild pain in the lower limbs, and intermittent claudication over the past 12 months, with no history of trauma, surgery, COVID-19 infection, influenza, or other infection. Visual acuity was light perception OD and no light perception OS. Both pupils dilated, with the right eye reacting sluggishly to light and the left eye being nonreactive. Intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg OD and 11 mm Hg OS. Posterior examination revealed optic disc edema in each eye, and the left eye had a swollen and pale optic disc with segmental blood flow in retinal vessels (Figure 1A). Fluorescein angiography of the left eye had prolonged arm-to-retina circulation time and multiple microaneurysms at the superotemporal and inferotemporal retina (Figure 1B). Visual evoked potentials were negative in both eyes. She had an increased white blood cell count (10 540/μL; to convert to ×109per liter, multiply by 0.001) and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (73 mm/h) and had positive findings for cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody and antinuclear antibody. Other serology test results were negative, including hepatitis B and C virus, HIV, rapid plasma reagin, and anti–double-stranded DNA.

case_info.explanation: C. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging For bilateral optic edema, ocular infection should be considered. The most clinically relevant slitlamp findings of the patient were optic disc edema in both eyes and abnormal pupil reaction to the light with no sign of infection. Her blood test results did not suggest systemic infection; therefore, a diagnostic intravitreal tap (choice A) would not be a preferred next step. Providing intravitreal corticosteroids (choice B) would not address the systemic symptoms, and no obvious retinal vascular inflammatory abnormalities were noted on fluorescein angiography. The patient had no family history of inherited genetic disorders to warrant genetic testing (choice D). The patient reported fatigue, occasional dizziness and headache, mild pain in her lower limbs, and intermittent claudication and had findings of elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and antinuclear antibody, suggesting the need for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (choice C). Brain MRI showed an abnormally high signal intensity in the left periventricular white matter (Figure 2) and was suspicious for a left middle cerebral artery infarct. Since MRI showed features consistent with a demyelinating disorder or local cerebral infarction in the left periventricular white matter, suggesting a systemic disease rather than optic neuritis, urgent referral to rheumatology was recommended for further investigation of systemic autoimmune diseases. The rheumatologist suspected Takayasu arteritis and arranged magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and arterial angiography for the head and neck. Both MRA and arterial angiography showed left common carotid artery and internal carotid artery occlusion, with right innominate artery and right common carotid artery stenosis, distal arterial occlusion, and multiple collateral arteries to the brain parenchyma (Figure 2), confirming a diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Subsequently, 400 mg of prednisone was given intravenously for 3 days. After 1 day, visual acuity improved to 20/32 OD and remained substantially impaired at hand motions OS, without further improvement. Takayasu arteritis is a rare autoimmune disease associated with inflammation of large vessels, such as the aorta and its main branches. It is known as pulseless disease and occurs commonly in young Asian women younger than 40 years.1Diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis may be challenging with lack of specific clinical symptoms and sensitive laboratory tests.2It is usually asymptomatic in the early stage, gradually proceeding to ischemic complications. Chronic ischemia can be associated with various clinical presentations, depending on the pattern of arterial involvement.3,4 Only approximately 9.6% cases present with vision loss as an initial clinical feature.5A comprehensive medical history and detailed physical examinations could provide valuable information to direct subsequent investigations. Diagnostic criteria for Takayasu arteritis consist of findings from imaging, laboratory tests, and physical examinations, eg, subclavian artery lesion, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and carotid artery tenderness.6On diagnosis, prompt and aggressive treatment using glucocorticoid therapy along with conventional immunosuppressive agents should be initiated, and surgical revascularization may be considered.7,8Long-term follow-up is recommended, especially for younger patients, due to a high relapse rate.9 After approximately 4 weeks of treatment, the patient’s dosage of glucocorticoid had been reduced to daily oral methylprednisolone acetate, 20 mg, along with oral methotrexate, 10 mg once per week. Her visual acuity remains 20/32 OD and counting fingers OS, and her physical symptoms have resolved.

case_info.explanation: C. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging For bilateral optic edema, ocular infection should be considered. The most clinically relevant slitlamp findings of the patient were optic disc edema in both eyes and abnormal pupil reaction to the light with no sign of infection. Her blood test results did not suggest systemic infection; therefore, a diagnostic intravitreal tap (choice A) would not be a preferred next step. Providing intravitreal corticosteroids (choice B) would not address the systemic symptoms, and no obvious retinal vascular inflammatory abnormalities were noted on fluorescein angiography. The patient had no family history of inherited genetic disorders to warrant genetic testing (choice D). The patient reported fatigue, occasional dizziness and headache, mild pain in her lower limbs, and intermittent claudication and had findings of elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and antinuclear antibody, suggesting the need for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (choice C). Brain MRI showed an abnormally high signal intensity in the left periventricular white matter (Figure 2) and was suspicious for a left middle cerebral artery infarct. Since MRI showed features consistent with a demyelinating disorder or local cerebral infarction in the left periventricular white matter, suggesting a systemic disease rather than optic neuritis, urgent referral to rheumatology was recommended for further investigation of systemic autoimmune diseases. The rheumatologist suspected Takayasu arteritis and arranged magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and arterial angiography for the head and neck. Both MRA and arterial angiography showed left common carotid artery and internal carotid artery occlusion, with right innominate artery and right common carotid artery stenosis, distal arterial occlusion, and multiple collateral arteries to the brain parenchyma (Figure 2), confirming a diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Subsequently, 400 mg of prednisone was given intravenously for 3 days. After 1 day, visual acuity improved to 20/32 OD and remained substantially impaired at hand motions OS, without further improvement. Takayasu arteritis is a rare autoimmune disease associated with inflammation of large vessels, such as the aorta and its main branches. It is known as pulseless disease and occurs commonly in young Asian women younger than 40 years.1Diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis may be challenging with lack of specific clinical symptoms and sensitive laboratory tests.2It is usually asymptomatic in the early stage, gradually proceeding to ischemic complications. Chronic ischemia can be associated with various clinical presentations, depending on the pattern of arterial involvement.3,4 Only approximately 9.6% cases present with vision loss as an initial clinical feature.5A comprehensive medical history and detailed physical examinations could provide valuable information to direct subsequent investigations. Diagnostic criteria for Takayasu arteritis consist of findings from imaging, laboratory tests, and physical examinations, eg, subclavian artery lesion, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and carotid artery tenderness.6On diagnosis, prompt and aggressive treatment using glucocorticoid therapy along with conventional immunosuppressive agents should be initiated, and surgical revascularization may be considered.7,8Long-term follow-up is recommended, especially for younger patients, due to a high relapse rate.9 After approximately 4 weeks of treatment, the patient’s dosage of glucocorticoid had been reduced to daily oral methylprednisolone acetate, 20 mg, along with oral methotrexate, 10 mg once per week. Her visual acuity remains 20/32 OD and counting fingers OS, and her physical symptoms have resolved.

You are a deliberation POLICY steering a conversation between a medical AI and a clinician toward
the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

Output STRICT JSON only:
{{

The patient reported fatigue, occasional dizziness and headache, mild pain in her lower limbs, and intermittent claudication and had findings of elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and antinuclear antibody, suggesting the need for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (choice C). Brain MRI showed an abnormally high signal intensity in the left periventricular white matter (Figure 2) and was suspicious for a left middle cerebral artery infarct. Since MRI showed features consistent with a demyelinating disorder or local cerebral infarction in the left periventricular white matter, suggesting a systemic disease rather than optic neuritis, urgent referral to rheumatology was recommended for further investigation of systemic autoimmune diseases. The rheumatologist suspected Takayasu arteritis and arranged magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and arterial angiography for the head and neck. Both MRA and arterial angiography showed left common carotid artery and internal carotid artery occlusion, with right innominate artery and right common carotid artery stenosis, distal arterial occlusion, and multiple collateral arteries to the brain parenchyma (Figure 2), confirming a diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Subsequently, 400 mg of prednisone was given intravenously for 3 days. After 1 day, visual acuity improved to 20/32 OD and remained substantially impaired at hand motions OS, without further improvement. Takayasu arteritis is a rare autoimmune disease associated with inflammation of large vessels, such as the aorta and its main branches. It is known as pulseless disease and occurs commonly in young Asian women younger than 40 years.1Diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis may be challenging with lack of specific clinical symptoms and sensitive laboratory tests.2It is usually asymptomatic in the early stage, gradually proceeding to ischemic complications. Chronic ischemia can be associated with various clinical presentations, depending on the pattern of arterial involvement.3,4 Only approximately 9.6% cases present with vision loss as an initial clinical feature.5A comprehensive medical history and detailed physical examinations could provide valuable information to direct subsequent investigations. Diagnostic criteria for Takayasu arteritis consist of findings from imaging, laboratory tests, and physical examinations, eg, subclavian artery lesion, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and carotid artery tenderness.6On diagnosis, prompt and aggressive treatment using glucocorticoid therapy along with conventional immunosuppressive agents should be initiated, and surgical revascularization may be considered.7,8Long-term follow-up is recommended, especially for younger patients, due to a high relapse rate.9 After approximately 4 weeks of treatment, the patient’s dosage of glucocorticoid had been reduced to daily oral methylprednisolone acetate, 20 mg, along with oral methotrexate, 10 mg once per week. Her visual acuity remains 20/32 OD and counting fingers OS, and her physical symptoms have resolved.

The patient reported fatigue, occasional dizziness and headache, mild pain in her lower limbs, and intermittent claudication and had findings of elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and antinuclear antibody, suggesting the need for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (choice C). Brain MRI showed an abnormally high signal intensity in the left periventricular white matter (Figure 2) and was suspicious for a left middle cerebral artery infarct. Since MRI showed features consistent with a demyelinating disorder or local cerebral infarction in the left periventricular white matter, suggesting a systemic disease rather than optic neuritis, urgent referral to rheumatology was recommended for further investigation of systemic autoimmune diseases. The rheumatologist suspected Takayasu arteritis and arranged magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and arterial angiography for the head and neck. She reported constant fatigue, occasional dizziness and headache, mild pain in the lower limbs, and intermittent claudication over the past 12 months, with no history of trauma, surgery, COVID-19 infection, influenza, or other infection. Visual acuity was light perception OD and no light perception OS. Both pupils dilated, with the right eye reacting sluggishly to light and the left eye being nonreactive. Intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg OD and 11 mm Hg OS. Posterior examination revealed optic disc edema in each eye, and the left eye had a swollen and pale optic disc with segmental blood flow in retinal vessels (Figure 1A). Fluorescein angiography of the left eye had prolonged arm-to-retina circulation time and multiple microaneurysms at the superotemporal and inferotemporal retina (Figure 1B). Visual evoked potentials were negative in both eyes. She had an increased white blood cell count (10 540/μL; to convert to ×109per liter, multiply by 0.001) and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (73 mm/h) and had positive findings for cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody and antinuclear antibody. Other serology test results were negative, including hepatitis B and C virus, HIV, rapid plasma reagin, and anti–double-stranded DNA.

Her blood test results did not suggest systemic infection; therefore, a diagnostic intravitreal tap (choice A) would not be a preferred next step. Providing intravitreal corticosteroids (choice B) would not address the systemic symptoms, and no obvious retinal vascular inflammatory abnormalities were noted on fluorescein angiography. The patient had no family history of inherited genetic disorders to warrant genetic testing (choice D). The patient reported fatigue, occasional dizziness and headache, mild pain in her lower limbs, and intermittent claudication and had findings of elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and antinuclear antibody, suggesting the need for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (choice C). Brain MRI showed an abnormally high signal intensity in the left periventricular white matter (Figure 2) and was suspicious for a left middle cerebral artery infarct. Since MRI showed features consistent with a demyelinating disorder or local cerebral infarction in the left periventricular white matter, suggesting a systemic disease rather than optic neuritis, urgent referral to rheumatology was recommended for further investigation of systemic autoimmune diseases. The rheumatologist suspected Takayasu arteritis and arranged magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and arterial angiography for the head and neck. Both MRA and arterial angiography showed left common carotid artery and internal carotid artery occlusion, with right innominate artery and right common carotid artery stenosis, distal arterial occlusion, and multiple collateral arteries to the brain parenchyma (Figure 2), confirming a diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Subsequently, 400 mg of prednisone was given intravenously for 3 days. After 1 day, visual acuity improved to 20/32 OD and remained substantially impaired at hand motions OS, without further improvement. Takayasu arteritis is a rare autoimmune disease associated with inflammation of large vessels, such as the aorta and its main branches. It is known as pulseless disease and occurs commonly in young Asian women younger than 40 years.1Diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis may be challenging with lack of specific clinical symptoms and sensitive laboratory tests.2It is usually asymptomatic in the early stage, gradually proceeding to ischemic complications. Chronic ischemia can be associated with various clinical presentations, depending on the pattern of arterial involvement.3,4 Only approximately 9.6% cases present with vision loss as an initial clinical feature.5A comprehensive medical history and detailed physical examinations could provide valuable information to direct subsequent investigations. Diagnostic criteria for Takayasu arteritis consist of findings from imaging, laboratory tests, and physical examinations, eg, subclavian artery lesion, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and carotid artery tenderness.6On diagnosis, prompt and aggressive treatment using glucocorticoid therapy along with conventional immunosuppressive agents should be initiated, and surgical revascularization may be considered.7,8Long-term follow-up is recommended, especially for younger patients, due to a high relapse rate.9 After approximately 4 weeks of treatment, the patient’s dosage of glucocorticoid had been reduced to daily oral methylprednisolone acetate, 20 mg, along with oral methotrexate, 10 mg once per week. Her visual acuity remains 20/32 OD and counting fingers OS, and her physical symptoms have resolved.

Case:
A 14-year old girl presented with sudden painless vision decline in the left eye for 5 days, without vision decline in the right eye. Her visual acuity was 20/20 OU 6 months earlier. She reported constant fatigue, occasional dizziness and headache, mild pain in the lower limbs, and intermittent claudication over the past 12 months, with no history of trauma, surgery, COVID-19 infection, influenza, or other infection. Visual acuity was light perception OD and no light perception OS. Both pupils dilated, with the right eye reacting sluggishly to light and the left eye being nonreactive. Intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg OD and 11 mm Hg OS. Posterior examination revealed optic disc edema in each eye, and the left eye had a swollen and pale optic disc with segmental blood flow in retinal vessels (Figure 1A). Fluorescein angiography of the left eye had prolonged arm-to-retina circulation time and multiple microaneurysms at the superotemporal and inferotemporal retina (Figure 1B). Visual evoked potentials were negative in both eyes. She had an increased white blood cell count (10 540/μL; to convert to ×109per liter, multiply by 0.001) and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (73 mm/h) and had positive findings for cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody and antinuclear antibody. Other serology test results were negative, including hepatitis B and C virus, HIV, rapid plasma reagin, and anti–double-stranded DNA.

  A. Perform diagnostic anterior chamber and/or vitreous tap
  B. Initiate intravitreal corticosteroids
  C. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging
  D. Arrange a genetic test

Let's proceed with the MRI for a comprehensive evaluation.

case_info.explanation: C. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging For bilateral optic edema, ocular infection should be considered. The most clinically relevant slitlamp findings of the patient were optic disc edema in both eyes and abnormal pupil reaction to the light with no sign of infection. Her blood test results did not suggest systemic infection; therefore, a diagnostic intravitreal tap (choice A) would not be a preferred next step. Providing intravitreal corticosteroids (choice B) would not address the systemic symptoms, and no obvious retinal vascular inflammatory abnormalities were noted on fluorescein angiography. The patient had no family history of inherited genetic disorders to warrant genetic testing (choice D). The patient reported fatigue, occasional dizziness and headache, mild pain in her lower limbs, and intermittent claudication and had findings of elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and antinuclear antibody, suggesting the need for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (choice C). Brain MRI showed an abnormally high signal intensity in the left periventricular white matter (Figure 2) and was suspicious for a left middle cerebral artery infarct. Since MRI showed features consistent with a demyelinating disorder or local cerebral infarction in the left periventricular white matter, suggesting a systemic disease rather than optic neuritis, urgent referral to rheumatology was recommended for further investigation of systemic autoimmune diseases. The rheumatologist suspected Takayasu arteritis and arranged magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and arterial angiography for the head and neck. Both MRA and arterial angiography showed left common carotid artery and internal carotid artery occlusion, with right innominate artery and right common carotid artery stenosis, distal arterial occlusion, and multiple collateral arteries to the brain parenchyma (Figure 2), confirming a diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Subsequently, 400 mg of prednisone was given intravenously for 3 days. After 1 day, visual acuity improved to 20/32 OD and remained substantially impaired at hand motions OS, without further improvement. Takayasu arteritis is a rare autoimmune disease associated with inflammation of large vessels, such as the aorta and its main branches. It is known as pulseless disease and occurs commonly in young Asian women younger than 40 years.1Diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis may be challenging with lack of specific clinical symptoms and sensitive laboratory tests.2It is usually asymptomatic in the early stage, gradually proceeding to ischemic complications. Chronic ischemia can be associated with various clinical presentations, depending on the pattern of arterial involvement.3,4 Only approximately 9.6% cases present with vision loss as an initial clinical feature.5A comprehensive medical history and detailed physical examinations could provide valuable information to direct subsequent investigations. Diagnostic criteria for Takayasu arteritis consist of findings from imaging, laboratory tests, and physical examinations, eg, subclavian artery lesion, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and carotid artery tenderness.6On diagnosis, prompt and aggressive treatment using glucocorticoid therapy along with conventional immunosuppressive agents should be initiated, and surgical revascularization may be considered.7,8Long-term follow-up is recommended, especially for younger patients, due to a high relapse rate.9 After approximately 4 weeks of treatment, the patient’s dosage of glucocorticoid had been reduced to daily oral methylprednisolone acetate, 20 mg, along with oral methotrexate, 10 mg once per week. Her visual acuity remains 20/32 OD and counting fingers OS, and her physical symptoms have resolved.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

case_info.scenario: A 14-year old girl presented with sudden painless vision decline in the left eye for 5 days, without vision decline in the right eye. Her visual acuity was 20/20 OU 6 months earlier. She reported constant fatigue, occasional dizziness and headache, mild pain in the lower limbs, and intermittent claudication over the past 12 months, with no history of trauma, surgery, COVID-19 infection, influenza, or other infection. Visual acuity was light perception OD and no light perception OS. Both pupils dilated, with the right eye reacting sluggishly to light and the left eye being nonreactive. Intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg OD and 11 mm Hg OS. Posterior examination revealed optic disc edema in each eye, and the left eye had a swollen and pale optic disc with segmental blood flow in retinal vessels (Figure 1A). Fluorescein angiography of the left eye had prolonged arm-to-retina circulation time and multiple microaneurysms at the superotemporal and inferotemporal retina (Figure 1B). Visual evoked potentials were negative in both eyes. She had an increased white blood cell count (10 540/μL; to convert to ×109per liter, multiply by 0.001) and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (73 mm/h) and had positive findings for cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody and antinuclear antibody. Other serology test results were negative, including hepatitis B and C virus, HIV, rapid plasma reagin, and anti–double-stranded DNA.

case_info.explanation: C. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging For bilateral optic edema, ocular infection should be considered. The most clinically relevant slitlamp findings of the patient were optic disc edema in both eyes and abnormal pupil reaction to the light with no sign of infection. Her blood test results did not suggest systemic infection; therefore, a diagnostic intravitreal tap (choice A) would not be a preferred next step. Providing intravitreal corticosteroids (choice B) would not address the systemic symptoms, and no obvious retinal vascular inflammatory abnormalities were noted on fluorescein angiography. The patient had no family history of inherited genetic disorders to warrant genetic testing (choice D). The patient reported fatigue, occasional dizziness and headache, mild pain in her lower limbs, and intermittent claudication and had findings of elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and antinuclear antibody, suggesting the need for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (choice C). Brain MRI showed an abnormally high signal intensity in the left periventricular white matter (Figure 2) and was suspicious for a left middle cerebral artery infarct. Since MRI showed features consistent with a demyelinating disorder or local cerebral infarction in the left periventricular white matter, suggesting a systemic disease rather than optic neuritis, urgent referral to rheumatology was recommended for further investigation of systemic autoimmune diseases. The rheumatologist suspected Takayasu arteritis and arranged magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and arterial angiography for the head and neck. Both MRA and arterial angiography showed left common carotid artery and internal carotid artery occlusion, with right innominate artery and right common carotid artery stenosis, distal arterial occlusion, and multiple collateral arteries to the brain parenchyma (Figure 2), confirming a diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Subsequently, 400 mg of prednisone was given intravenously for 3 days. After 1 day, visual acuity improved to 20/32 OD and remained substantially impaired at hand motions OS, without further improvement. Takayasu arteritis is a rare autoimmune disease associated with inflammation of large vessels, such as the aorta and its main branches. It is known as pulseless disease and occurs commonly in young Asian women younger than 40 years.1Diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis may be challenging with lack of specific clinical symptoms and sensitive laboratory tests.2It is usually asymptomatic in the early stage, gradually proceeding to ischemic complications. Chronic ischemia can be associated with various clinical presentations, depending on the pattern of arterial involvement.3,4 Only approximately 9.6% cases present with vision loss as an initial clinical feature.5A comprehensive medical history and detailed physical examinations could provide valuable information to direct subsequent investigations. Diagnostic criteria for Takayasu arteritis consist of findings from imaging, laboratory tests, and physical examinations, eg, subclavian artery lesion, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and carotid artery tenderness.6On diagnosis, prompt and aggressive treatment using glucocorticoid therapy along with conventional immunosuppressive agents should be initiated, and surgical revascularization may be considered.7,8Long-term follow-up is recommended, especially for younger patients, due to a high relapse rate.9 After approximately 4 weeks of treatment, the patient’s dosage of glucocorticoid had been reduced to daily oral methylprednisolone acetate, 20 mg, along with oral methotrexate, 10 mg once per week. Her visual acuity remains 20/32 OD and counting fingers OS, and her physical symptoms have resolved.
